newsitem.title: USA: Ivax Corp falls on earnings, resignation.
newsitem.headline: Ivax Corp falls on earnings, resignation.

text.p: IVAX Corp shares fell sharply Monday following the generic drugmaker's twin announcements late Friday of a steep earnings loss in the second quarter and the resignation of its president and chief operating officer, Robert Strauss.
Shares were off 2-1/16 to 9 in afternoon trade.

The Miami-based company reported a 1997 second-quarter net loss of $47.5 million, or $0.39 a share, after the close Friday. It posted losses from continuing operations of $52.8 million, or 43 cents a share, in stark contrast to Wall Street expectations of break-even results for the quarter.
IVAX reported a $20.5 million charge in the second quarter related primarily to a consolidation-related writedown of assets at its U.S. generic drugs division, Zenith Goldline.

"There was a huge earnings shortfall for the quarter," said Oppenheimer & Co pharmaceuticals analyst Michael Krensavage, who added the company has been unable to win approvals for enough generic drugs to resurrect earnings that have flagged for most of the past year.
"They have won approvals, but not large enough ones to put their troubles behind them," Krensavage said.
He said IVAX is still braving financial woes from having booked revenues for excessively large shipments of drugs to wholesalers in the 1996 first quarter.
"Prices of the drugs plummeted because of competition from other drug companies and Ivax had to give customer credits," Krensavage said.
"The company has not been able to turn around" from its problems, he said, with Strauss bowing out only four months after being hired to revamp operations.
Strauss said Friday his decision to resign was "a matter of differing management styles and vision for the company," adding his relations remained amicable with chief executive Phillip Frost.

"The resignation doesn't distress me because IVAX hasn't had very good results from its management for the last three or four years," said Thom Brown, drug analyst for Rutherford Brown & Catherwood. "It's been on a downhill trend because it hasn't been able to cope with changing trends and pricing pressures in the generic drug business."
Brown described Frost as "a talented dealmaker.
"But I don't think his talent lies in day-to-day management," he said.
